issues.legal_issue: A prior decision upholding a statute does not preclude a fresh challenge to Parliament’s legislative competence when that specific question was not debated in the prior case.
material_facts: An earlier Constitution Bench had upheld the statute’s constitutionality, but its decision did not discuss which legislative-list entry empowered Parliament to enact it.
The petitioner’s renewed constitutional challenge specifically contended that the subject matter fell within the State List and outside Parliament’s legislative competence.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner was not barred from raising the legislative-competence challenge by the earlier decision.
issues.legal_principle: In Hari Singh v. Military Estate Officer (1973), the Court had upheld the statute, but the legislative-competence question was not debated and the judgment gave no analysis of the relevant legislative entries. The Court therefore did not treat that decision as foreclosing the distinct challenge raised here.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A litigant brings a constitutional writ challenge to the validity of a law.
predicates.earlier_decision_upheld_law: An earlier court decision upheld the law’s validity.
predicates.competence_issue_not_debated_before: The earlier decision did not debate the specific question of the legislature’s authority to enact the law.
predicates.challenge_not_precluded: The new challenge is not barred by the earlier decision.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenge follows an earlier decision upholding the law, the challenge is not barred if legislative competence was not debated earlier.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament has authority to provide a speedy procedure for eviction of unauthorised occupants from property belonging to the Union.
material_facts: The statute’s central subject was a speedy procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants from public premises.
The petitioner argued that the subject belonged to the State List and that Parliament lacked authority to legislate on it.

The Court found no State legislation shown to govern speedy eviction of unauthorised occupants from property belonging to the Union, and held that any such Parliamentary legislation would prevail over State legislation concerning Union property.
issues.conclusion: The statute’s provisions for speedy eviction from Union property fall within Parliament’s legislative competence.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the pith-and-substance test, the Court identified the statute’s subject as providing a speedy procedure for eviction of unauthorised occupants from public premises, as stated in Hari Singh v. Military Estate Officer (1973). Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive authority over matters in the Union List. Entry 32 of List I covers Union property and revenue from it; although a State may legislate concerning Union property situated within it, Parliamentary legislation on that property prevails. The Court held that Entry 32 was wide enough to cover eviction legislation and therefore did not need to decide the scope of Entry 18 of List II. It also distinguished the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, which concerned tenants of non-government landlords rather than speedy eviction of unauthorised occupants from Union property. Indu Bhushan Bose v. Ram Sundari (1970) was cited on the meaning of the landlord-and-tenant entry.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A litigant challenges the constitutional validity of a law providing for eviction from public premises.
predicates.speedy_eviction_law: The law provides a speedy procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants.
predicates.union_property_is_subject: The property to which the eviction law applies belongs to the Union.

issues.definition: If a constitutional validity challenge concerns a law providing speedy eviction of unauthorised occupants from Union property, Parliament has legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament has authority to provide for speedy eviction of unauthorised occupants from property belonging to a government company in which the Central Government holds a majority of the paid-up capital.
material_facts: The statute’s definition of public premises included premises belonging to or taken on lease by a company in which the Central Government held at least 51 per cent of the paid-up capital.
The petitioner challenged Parliament’s authority to legislate concerning premises belonging to a government company.

The Court concluded that the State and Concurrent Lists did not cover the subject of speedy eviction from such company property and that Parliament could legislate for government companies, including companies with property in different States.
issues.conclusion: Parliament had legislative competence to provide for speedy eviction of unauthorised occupants from the covered government-company property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Entry 43 of List I concerning companies and on the residuary authority in Entry 97 of List I, read with Entry 95 concerning courts’ jurisdiction and powers. It concluded that no relevant State- or Concurrent-List entry had been shown to cover speedy eviction from the property of a government company. The Court agreed with the reasoning in L.S. Nair v. Hindustan Steel Ltd. (Madhya Pradesh High Court, 1980), which had considered Entries 43 and 95 of List I and Entries 6, 7 and 46 of List III. The Court also noted that the Indian Companies Act itself was enacted under Entry 43 of List I.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and government_company_property and central_government_holds_majority_capital and no_state_or_concurrent_entry_covers_subject

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A litigant challenges the constitutional validity of a law that provides for eviction from public premises.
predicates.government_company_property: The law applies to premises belonging to or taken on lease by a government company.
predicates.central_government_holds_majority_capita: The Central Government holds a majority of the company’s paid-up capital.
predicates.no_state_or_concurrent_entry_covers_subj: No matter in the State or Concurrent List covers the subject of speedy eviction from the company’s property.

issues.definition: If a constitutional validity challenge concerns speedy eviction from government-company property, the Central Government holds a majority of the company’s paid-up capital, and no State- or Concurrent-List matter covers the subject, Parliament has legislative competence.
